title: Exploring how to offer weight management advice and support during dermatology appointments
official: EMBED: embedded brief weight-management in dermatology trial
summary:
Background and study aims
People with psoriasis are more likely to live with excess weight, which can make their psoriasis worse and reduce how well some treatments work. Research suggests that losing weight can improve psoriasis symptoms and quality of life. However, weight management is not routinely discussed during dermatology appointments. Healthcare professionals may have limited time or feel uncomfortable raising the topic with patients.

Working closely with patients and healthcare professionals, the study team have developed a short conversation guide to help dermatology clinicians discuss the link between psoriasis and weight, explain the potential benefits of weight management, and offer referral to appropriate weight-management support.

This study aims to find out whether this approach is practical to deliver during routine dermatology appointments and acceptable to patients and healthcare professionals. It will also find out whether it would be possible to carry out a larger study in the future to assess how effective this approach is.

Who can participate?
Adults with psoriasis who are living with excess weight and attending one of two participating dermatology clinics.

What does the study involve?
People who agree to take part will be asked to complete some initial assessments, most of which can be done remotely. Height and weight will be measured during a routine dermatology clinic visit to confirm eligibility.

Participants will then be randomly allocated to one of two groups, with twice as many people receiving the new approach as receiving usual care.

Group 1 – Brief weight-management conversation and support: Participants will have a short conversation with a dermatology healthcare professional about the link between psoriasis and weight management. They will also be offered a referral to an appropriate weight-management programme. There will be a short remote follow-up after four weeks.
Taking up the offer of a referral and attending a weight-management programme are entirely optional.

Group 2 – Usual care: Participants will continue to receive their usual psoriasis care, which may include general advice about healthy lifestyles.

After 12 weeks, participants in both groups will be asked to repeat some of the initial assessments. These will mostly be completed remotely to minimise the time and travel involved. Each participant will be involved in the study for approximately 12 weeks.

With their permission, some participants will also have their conversations audio-recorded or be invited to take part in an interview about their experiences. Some healthcare professionals will also be interviewed to understand how well the approach works in everyday clinical practice.

The main focus of this study is to find out whether the new approach is practical and acceptable, rather than to test whether it leads to weight loss. The findings will help us decide whether and how to carry out a larger study in the future.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
People receiving the new approach may benefit from a better understanding of how weight can affect psoriasis and from being offered support to manage their weight. 

Some people may find conversations about weight uncomfortable or sensitive. Healthcare professionals delivering the intervention will be supported to approach these discussions respectfully and sensitively. Participants can choose whether to accept a referral for further weight-management support.

Taking part will also involve some additional assessments, which may require a small amount of time. Most assessments will be completed remotely to reduce inconvenience, and participants will be provided with shopping vouchers as a thank-you for their time.

Although participants may not benefit directly, the findings could help improve how weight-management support is offered to people with psoriasis in the future.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being coordinated by the University of Oxford and will recruit participants from two dermatology clinics at Oxford University Hospitals and King’s College Hospital. 

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2027 to 11 July 2028.

Who is funding the study?
The National Institute for Health Research (NIHR), UK. 

Who is the main contact?
Dr. Sarah Morrow, University of Oxford, sarah.morrow@phc.ox.ac.uk.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patient inclusion criteria:
1. Participant is willing and able to give informed consent for participation in the study
2. Aged 18 years or above
3. BMI > =  25 kg/m2 (BMI > =  27 kg/m2 if white ethnicity)
4. Established diagnosis of psoriasis

Clinician inclusion criteria (interviews only):
1. Health care professional participant is willing and able to give informed consent for participation in the study
2. Involved in the trial through delivery of the intervention / usual care
Exclusion criteria:
The (patient) participant may not enter the study if ANY of the following apply:
1. Female participant who is pregnant, lactating or planning to become pregnant during the course of the trial
2. Currently participating in a structured weight loss programme; use of weight-loss medications within the previous 3 months; or > = 10% self‐reported weight loss in the 6 months before baseline
3. Any other significant disease or disorder which, in the opinion of the Investigator, may either put the participants at risk because of participation in the trial, influence the results of the trial, or affect the participant’s ability to take part
